stages.a: A colonized block. An X is cut through the bag on its face.
stages.v: Little detailed data exists for pink oyster: treat it like the other oysters.

stages.a: Pins crowd out through the cut.
stages.v: Made for heat: a grower whose greenhouse ran 27-32 °C was still turning out oysters. In hot places, start with pinks.

stages.a: Thin, frilled caps crowd into a rosette. Their edges still roll under.
stages.v: High CO2 gives long stems and no caps. Watch stem length and cap shape as your airflow gauge.

stages.a: The caps open out, thin and frilled at the edge.
stages.v: Oysters are picked before the caps flatten.

stages.a: The caps flatten and the frilled edges lift.
stages.v: Pinks look pretty but do not hold up in the pan, and old pinks smell bad in the bin. Sell them fast.

stages.a: The edges turn up and split, and the gills shed spores.
stages.v: Spore load matters for staff health.

labels.a: The cut in the bag. The cluster comes out here.
labels.v: Treat pinks like other oysters: blue oysters are opened with side slits or X cuts.

labels.a: A crowded knot of pins at the cut.
labels.v: Blotch shows first on the centre pin of a budding cluster, and on aborted pins at its base.

labels.a: Short stems, joined at the base.
labels.v: Short stems mean good airflow. High CO2 gives long stems with small caps or none.

labels.a: Pink oyster caps are thin, with a wavy, frilled edge.
Gills run down from the cap onto the stem.
The cap opens flat and its edge lifts.
labels.v: Pick before the caps flatten. Pinks keep badly, so sell them fast.

labels.a: The edge curls up and splits as the cap ages.
Spores drift down from the gills.
labels.v: Spore load matters for staff health.
